blocks.x: I'll make an announcement here that we're recording an interview at 612 Prierre Street. How do you say this street? Prierre. Prierre. Prierre Street. Yeah, Prierre. In New Orleans on August the 11th, 1960. And can you give your name, your full name, Mr. Kelly? Ben Kelly. How do you spell your last name?
Ben Kelly.
I didn't know if there was an E in there at the end, just L-L-Y at the end. Well, yeah. Can you tell us just when you were born, your birth date? My birthday?
My birthday would be Christmas the 25th. I'd be 60 years old. 60?
80 years old. 80? That's what I thought. Somebody said you'd be about 80 years old.
80 years old.

Mr. Sidney Brown, who came over yesterday, said you were about 80. He felt. I'd be 80 years old on Christmas the 25th. This coming Christmas. This coming Christmas. Next time. Born on Christmas Day, Mr. Kelly. Yes, sir. I believe Jim Robinson was born on Christmas Day, too. I think he was born on the same day. Well, he's younger. He's younger. Yeah, he's about... He's younger than me. About 67 or 68, something like that, this year. So, can you tell us just what town or what... Was that on the plantation down at Deer Ring?
That's right. On the plantation. Down at Deer Ring. The plantation.
Can you tell us, did your father or mother, anyone play music in your family?
No. No. My father never did play no music. And my mother didn't play no music. They was Christian, church members.
Yes. Did they sing in the church there?
Yeah.
What kind of a church? Was that a Baptist? Baptist church. Both of them was Baptist. Can you tell us that when you took up music, did you learn an instrument when you were a boy?
I learned when I was a young man, around 21, 22, 23 years old. What instrument did you take up?
Trombone. Trombone. Did you play in the band down there?
I played in the band. Brass band.
Yep, brass band. Was that the same one that Jim Robinson told us about, that they had old man Jim Humphrey came down as a teacher? Old man Jim Humphrey.
Valorant of Liberty. That's why he was. That was my professor. He teached me eyes and bones, pure ants and all of us.
Did you say that band was called the Elks? The Elks. Yeah. Elks brass band. That's right.

What kind of a trombone was it? Was it a slide or a valve? Valve. Had the valves on with it? At that time. Like a cornet. That's right. Can you tell us about your brother? Was he older or younger than you? He was younger than me, way younger than me. Chris was younger than me. Chris was younger than me.
About how many years was he younger than you?
I was younger than me. I was younger than me.
Chris was about 25 years, younger than me.
I got it packed up somewhere in there. But it would take me so long to find it. We got so many packages. It was deep down.

Yes, I know how many years. Was Chris born when you started to play the trombone? Huh? Was Chris born when you started to play your trombone? When I started playing trombone? Yeah. Was Chris born then? Yeah, a young boy. He was a little boy then? A little boy. Uh-huh.
He was something around 20 years or so younger than you then? Oh, sure. Yeah. Sure. Do you know when Chris died? What year it was when he died about?
No, I don't know exactly what, I lost the record of it. But I can get it.
Sometime we can find out. Maybe other people might have told us, remembered the funeral. I think it was around the 1930 period, wasn't it?
Yeah, yeah, yeah. He was buried down in Shalman Cemetery.
Oh, down there? Yeah, right there, Shalman. In the big, with all the soldiers and all? Yeah. Was he in the army during the First World War, do you remember?
Yeah, that's right. Got caught in there.
We could find his grave, I guess, it would tell on the tombstone too.
Oh yeah, you can't help him find his grave.
Did he have any middle name or initial? Chris Kelly?
That's all what I would know of the colony.
You know what his full name was? Is it Christopher or anything? Chris Kelly. Chris. Chris Kelly.
Chris, uh-huh. And you see it on the tomb? The headboat there, Chris Kelly.
We'll try to find it sometime.
That's his name, that's his full name.
Do you remember anything else about your brass band? Did they have parades down there when you were young?
Yeah. I played music down there, who they are, in the parades down there. They had the mason down there. But the mason was at Woodland.
Oh yes.

At a place below us called Woodland. I've heard of that. And we used to go down there and play the for rids and things. Bring them up further this way to the church and carry them back and dismiss them. And we'd come back on the dairy.
Magnolia plantation was near it. It was below that. It was down below. Yes, below that.
Magnolia plantation was below that.
Was it below Woodland too then? Magnolia? Uh-huh. Yeah. It was farther down the river. Sure. Sure, farther down. Do you remember how many you had in the band, about how big a band it was?
We had ten pieces now.
Ten pieces. How many trombones and how many cornets about do you remember?
We had three cornets. We had three cornets and we had two trombones. But there was key trombones. Yes.
Have alto horn and baritone or what else? Yeah.

We had solo alto and we had baritone and we had bass too. We had a first alto in our band. Bass drum and snare drum. Any clarinet? No. No clarinet? No. We didn't have no clarinet. We had a first tenor in our band. A brass instrument? Yes.
Something like a baritone was that?
Yes. That's right. How long did you play down in that band? When did you come up to New Orleans?
I played in that band until it broke up. You finally broke up then? Yes. And it broke up.
And you remember when that was? So many old heads would play in there and died out and went to different places and the band just went to finish.
Oh, do you remember Sonny Henry down that way? That's right. We knew him very well. Yes, that's right.
Sonny Henry. He died right up here. Last Christmas time, about January he died. Yeah, Sonny Henry. Sonny Henry, the field form, anarchy, the Irish bone. They all come from the same house.

When did you move here? Do you remember, was it the time of the First World War, before that or after the big storm? After the big storm. After that storm? After that big storm. In 1915, that storm. That's when I come here. And I've been here ever since. Did you play music when you came up here? Up here? Well I played music once, twice. I just got over. Put it down, teetot, all together.

And took up and went to work out there, put this big lumber yard out there on the feet in Robinson. We were a media in company. I get to the other boys. Oh yeah. And you see, I was up with that now. Out there. I got to be a night watcher out there. And it was like, you know, I was up with that. And I was up with that now. I got to be a night watcher out there. And I had nine keys to punch. And it was like, let me tell you if I was up with that now. I was up with that now. Yeah. I had a clock on me. I had to go to that place and put the key in there to register. If I missed the round, that cop would show me up. And I'd go to another place. Keys was all passed. I'd go there and put my key in and punch in. And the last place I'd come to punch again would be at the office. And I had that to do every hour. Every hour I had that to do. Rain and shine. I had them around with me. And you know what I would do? You see when seven o'clock come, you wish to go to work at seven o'clock. I'd get out there and go to work. Run home and get me a drink of coffee. Go there and unload that number. Everything. I had to do that to work. My children was all small. I done all that to raise my children. And I would say the day is time goes. I'm still young on the scene, but Lord take young.

Yes, you look very good health. You look very good health for your age. Lord take young health right now. Yes, indeed. Did you ever play the slide trombone at all? Did you ever try one? No. Never did play it? Just about.
No. Never did. Ain't gonna lie.
I never done did. Did your band down at the plantation, did they always use the music, the little books?

Yeah, of course. On the little cards. Yeah. The music on the little cards. Professor Umper used to write us, used to teach them. He'd write all those out for you. Yeah. Me, Sonny Henry, Piancen, Hyatt and Bone, he'd teach you all of us.

Do you remember any of the pieces, any of the marches or what kind of music you used, what the pieces were like? We had six eight pieces. Six eight marches and all. Six eight marches, that's how we used either for marches.
Six eight.
Did you ever play any spirituals or hymns down there?

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, we played hymns. That's all we used to play. Like a funeral at the church or anything like that. We'd go, we'd get a bar to bring it from the church. We never played no jazz music. We'd go to Christ or anything. When we did miss, we did miss the kids.
That's where we was today. Was there any special days in the week that you would play or would you play just on Sundays or any day? No.
Not just on a Sunday. We had different days we used to play. Like anybody wants to hire us or something like that.

We always had the privilege. We could get off and go and play. That's what we had. Did your band ever come up here for Mardi Gras or Carnival? Did you ever have any parades up in New Orleans? On Labor Day. Labor Day. Labor Day.
Labor Day we had parades up there. Your band would come up here?
Yeah.
For Labor Day. Yeah. We'd right there at the business at the Elk Street. At a hall that's called Elk. We used to meet there. All the bands used to meet up there together.
There was an old hall there at Globe Hall too, was there?
The Grove Hall was out there on St. Peter Street. St. Peter. Yeah. Out there near the basement. What they used to call it the basement. Yes. It was right off from that auditorium.
Right where the auditorium is. Yeah.
Right off.

Now you must be known up top of them. Yes, I never knew that hall. People tell us about that hall. Yeah. Used to call it the Grove Hall. Did you ever play any dance work any place for dances or just the brass band? Oh, brass band used to play the dances. They played the dances too? Sure.

Sure used to play the dances out there. Sometimes the brass band would play the dances and sometimes the string band played the dances. Jim Robinson and Jim Lindler and all them, we was playing in the old Chester band. Yeah, string band.
What kind of music did you use for the dance? Did you have any waltzes or what kind of music did they use?
They had waltzes and jazz. In jazz? Yes.
Did you ever play in a string band?
Nobody played in a string band. Nobody played in a string band. Nobody.

Nobody played in a string band. I was there always a string band there. Can you remember when it started or was there always a string band on Dave Ames there? What kind of string band did they have? Did they always have a string band there? string band band?

How far back, when you were a little boy, what kind of music did they have when you were a little boy, say seven or eight years old? Can you remember any kind of music you heard when you were, before you took up music? Mm-mm.
We didn't have anything. Not down there. Nothing down there?
No, not that way. Just the bass band?
Mm-hmm. I can't lie, they didn't have it down there, then.
Do you remember about when it was that they started that string band?
Can I remember when they started that string band? Yeah, was it after you took up music? Yeah.
Oh, it was after. Yeah. Yeah.
After. This boy was sitting around, he used to play the ambulance. Do you know that?
Mm-hmm.
Jim Robbins, who used to play that, and my brother Chris Kelly.
Can you tell, when did your brothers take up music? Can you remember about when it was, how old you were, or were you in the big band, of course?
Yeah, I was twenty, twenty-two years old. I know, twenty-two years old when he took up music.
When he took up music?
Yeah.
Or was that when you took up music? When did you take up music? How old were you about? Me?
Yes. I was a man around twenty-five, twenty-six years old. I took up music, very young.
And Chris, you say, Chris took up music when he was in his early twenties?
Yeah.
The late teens, early twenties, something like that? Yeah, sure. What instrument did he start with?
The trumpet.
Oh he did start with, started right in on that. On the trumpet. And did he play with your brass band?
Yeah. He did? Yeah. He played with the brass band.
And he was a fairly good reader, would you say?

He was a number one reader. He was. Really good. He was really good. You could get any piece of music you could put up there. He would look at it and cast his eye down on it. That was all right. He got it, son. Yeah. Yeah. But give him that. Who was him? Heisenborns, Peter Anderson, and well, see Sonny Henry, he was in my class. He was in there.
And he could really get it. Who was Chris' teacher? Did he have a teacher then too? Professor Umpham. He was, taught him too?
Yeah. Professor Umpham. From Valence and Liberty uptown. Yeah. That's where that is. Yes.

That was how. I know some of his, I know his son Willie the clarinetist and the- Yeah, Willie Umpham, he got one. And the grandchildren. Yeah. Percy and the young Willie, we know them very well. Ah. But we know them. But I never knew the old man Jim.

He lived on that side, that big white school up there, the valent school in that house and you could go in his house and you had an instrument and an old iron in his house. All around. Teach it to every an instrument you want. That's what he could do.
Yes, indeed. Did Chris take to the trumpet well? Did it take him a long time to learn the trumpet? No. Didn't take him long?

No, he always was apt and had plenty of brains. Uh huh. He was an apt youngster, he had plenty of brains. He'd hide him just like an eagle on a nose. I wish I could catch all the reeds and do something like he could.

How big was he about when he started? How big he was? Was he a boy or? No, a young man. He was 19 and 20 and like that. He didn't start when he was a little boy then? No. Well, you can say a young man.
Yeah, a young man rather than a boy. He was an 18-year-old boy then.
And he played with your brass band and then did he also play with the string band? Yeah. He played with the string band too. Yeah. Yeah. And uh.
Professor Humphrey always said, actually a little friend then, he wished he had everybody like that had the brains what he had.
He was a kind of a star pupil.

Yes, indeed. That Globe Hall, that economy hall where they got church at now. And round there on Liberty Street, the Isilon Street, when they say he was playing there, he couldn't get in that hole. Just made families and great like that.
About what year did he come to New Orleans, Mr. Kelly?
What year did he come to New Orleans?
Did he come the same time as you?
When I come to town?
Yeah. Did he come with you? No. Oh, he came before that? Yeah. Oh, he did come.
Sure.
Before you then.
Yeah. He came in here for four weeks.
About how long? A couple of years?
Yeah. He just got there, he got tired out there, he just picked up and left. He'd come over there and went to town.
And he just took up music when he came to New Orleans, did he, or did he do something? No.
No, he played down there.
He said he played down in the band, sure. I see, when he came to New Orleans, did he do anything else besides play music?
Yeah. Yeah.
What did he do?

Used to wake up in the Iron Yard up there on the Capitol between St. Gene and Market, 1662, 66. Oh, the Iron Yard. Yeah. In Markton's Sun. He'd do that in the daytime and play music at night. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Very good. Did you ever go to hear his band play? Yeah, plenty of time I was there with him. Yeah? He had played with my artists where I was blowing things. You remember, you know, we all talk at the Bulls Club? Oh yeah. Oh yeah. Still the Yard's Club uptown now. Yeah.
From Yard's Club.

Yeah. I was blowing things. Paul on that side, there was a woman on that side, band in the middle of it. Could dance every evening you were. Oh, very good. Yeah. Yeah. Do you remember who else was in Chris' band? How big a orchestra was? Or did you ever go to a club? I was blowing things. I was blowing things. Do you remember if I was talking to Bulls Club? Oh yeah. Oh yeah.
Still the Elks Club uptown now. Yeah. From the Elks Club. I was blowing things. Mm-hmm.
The Paul was on that side, there was a woman on that side. A band in the middle of it. Could dance every evening you were.
Oh, very good. Mm-hmm. That's right. Do you remember who else was in Chris' band? orchestra or his dance orchestra how big it was? Well, he had this boy in there called

Jim Robinson. He played with him in the band. He had this boy, Chita Howell. He come up, Chris taught him he used to be a drummer. My brother broke him off the drum. Put him on a trumpet and made him famous during this time. Who was the clarinet player with the band? Do you remember who played clarinet? Well, they had one fellow that had to try to play clarinet, but he never did make

famous so he just put it down. Do you remember his name? Yeah. Called him Norwood. What was the name again? No, Norwood. Norwood. Yeah. Oh, no. Norwood. But he put it down. He didn't stay with it? No. Do you remember who he had then later?

Didn't use no. Didn't use clarinet or something? No. All he used was trumpet, big instruments, baritone, solo alto, voice alto, drum. This is the brass band you're talking about? Yeah, the brass band. Now in the string band which they had, they used clarinet. But that's uh, he's dead and gone. That's uh, Jim Riddler, uncle. Sam Robinson. Oh, Sam Robinson. Yeah. That was the clarinet player. Was that a brother of Jim Robinson's, the trombonist, his brother? Yeah. His brother. Yeah. He told us a little bit about him. We never talked very much to him about his brother.

I know he's dead. I know he's dead. Long time. Yeah. Nice youngster. Nice youngster. Can you tell us uh, any more about Chris? People tell us that he used a lot of mute sometimes. Yeah. Or maybe a rubber plunger, you know, one of those rubber things. Yeah. Do you know when he picked those up when he started on that? Huh? When did he start to use those? Did he use those down the country too? No. Just after he come up here.

Mm-hmm. He never used that down the country. Mm-hmm. Nothing but the old instrument. But I'd be come up here and you'd see so many of them. From the head, them things with them muffles, mute, put up and all and so. Yeah. So he got one of them he used. Okay.
I've heard he said that he could make all kinds of freak effects almost like he was talking.

Mm-hmm. Yeah. And people used to tell him, you tell him when he gets to play, he starts murmuring out over there and they say, Oh, preach, preach. Come on out with it. Preach, preach. And Lord, Lord. And stuff like stuff stuff like stuff even a leftist town of the field.
It was good music to dance to, was it? Yeah. Nice beat to it?
Yeah, indeed, yes, fine music to dance.

People tell us that he played the blues so wonderful. Do you remember any of the blues that he played, what they were like, the name of them or anything? I can't remember the name, but I can remember some of the blues.
I've got to look around sometime, see if I can find that package. And they ought to have some of his music card up, a couple to run up on.
Oh, before I forget, do you happen to have a picture, a photograph of a person? Nobody, I've never seen a picture that I can remember.
No, I had one of these photographs, and that photograph just got this missing from you. And I inquired, and I wiped, but I could not find that picture.
It was too bad. I'd like to see a picture of him. Same way with Buddy Petit. Hardly anybody ever saved a picture of Buddy Petit.

I had one in that picture of somebody. Clipped that picture, I don't know. His wife over took it to work and moved and tell me about it. And I had been to her home, and I didn't wipe and watch on the fly. But I never did see. I never could find that picture.
Now, nowadays they can make copies of it. You know, they can make another photo and get more copies made. I hope that we could get a copy of a picture sometime of Chris.
I'm going to start to visit.
Maybe somebody will find one someday. Somebody must have taken one. Yeah. Somebody must have one in the whole city somewhere.
Yeah, I'm going to do the best I can for each time I'm going to find you one.
Yeah, it'd be nice if we could have one, and then we can make a copy of it, you see. And you can have the full of your facts.
And you remember one piece he played that tell me was Careless Love. Careless Love. Do you remember who played that?

Yeah. He played that. He composed that piece. He composed that piece. He composed that piece. Oh, my God. Could this boy say that he's playing. That's Careless Love. And when he started playing that heavy ball, all of them women, they say, oh, preacher, preacher, preacher, preacher, preacher. They're that tell his love. I'm telling you.
And that was a sort of a nickname he had, preacher. Huh? They call him preacher. They call him preacher.
He went like a preacher. And them women, they'd whoop and holler, oh, come on, preach, preach, preach.
Now, did he read music in the string band? Did he play from written music in the string band? That's right. That's right. And the way of music in the string band of music from the brass band.
And the way you could tell if she was just getting, come, put it down here, take a look at it like that.
Did all those string bands play from written music, Mr. Kelly? Mm-hmm.
And then? That's my uncle, teach all them bands down here. Strictly by music. Of course he used to pick up and play jazz music too. Oh, yeah. He didn't know they played music like that.
He used to play a folk song. Well, when he played jazz music, he didn't read the... No. No.

Is Chris's wife still living? Last time I heard from him she's living. He has a son too. I've never met him. You've met his son, haven't you? Yeah, I met his son. Yeah. That's his son. One called Jack.
Jack. That's right. Jack. I saw him but I don't know him.
Don't be his uncle. Yeah. Yeah. He'd be a friend. He's working downtown somewhere and she could play.
He's working. Well, while I think of it, did you have any other brothers that played any music? No one else in the family then that played music? No.
Did you ever play in Chris's band? What's called?
In the brass band.
Not in the string band? No. Can't tell that a lot. Oh, indeed. About how long did you play together in the brass band?
Oh, we played together pretty good wives in the brass band, but seven or eight children.
That was down in the country, down at the Deer Range. That's right. You got that right.
We used to left them at Deer Range and go over to send soap and paper read and things.
Is that on the other side of the river? No, since Hopi's on this side of the river. This side, yeah that's what I mean.
And Deer Rains on the other side. That's right. Can you remember other places that Chris played? You mentioned Economy Hall.
Yeah, where Griffin got church at that now, where Griffin got church?
Oh yes, that's the old Hopes Hall or Cooperators Hall. That's the Cooperated Hall. Was he sick long before he died? Do you remember when he died?
No, he didn't stay sick too long before he passed away.
What was his trouble? What did he die on from?
Well, he just died by dissipated little bit. He over dissipated something little bit.
Was he very old? Do you remember when he died? No, he wasn't really an old man when he died. I know he wouldn't be old. I mean, he was quite young then when he died. Sure.
Did he usually keep the same band all the time or did he have a different string band?
Well, right now all the time they had the same band.
And he had a clarinet in his band. Oh yeah? In the string band. Yeah.

Is there anything else you can remember about Chris or the band down there in the country? Anything you'd like to tell? No. I don't want to bother you much longer, but I thought if there's anything else. stuff
